summary: Reading simple assembly language programs (Little Man Computer instruction set) and using trace tables to follow and check algorithms.

blocks.content: Assembly language uses **mnemonics** for machine instructions. NIS papers use an instruction set like the **Little Man Computer (LMC)**: one **accumulator (ACC)**, memory locations 00–99, and these instructions:

blocks.title: Instruction set
rows: Load ACC with the contents of address xx
Branch to xx **if ACC ≥ 0** (zero or positive)
A memory location holding data n (not an instruction)

blocks.content:
00  INP          ; read N
01  STA 09       ; store N
02  LDA 09       ; loop: load N
03  BRZ 08       ; if N = 0 finish
04  OUT          ; output N
05  SUB 10       ; N - 1
06  STA 09       ; save the new N
07  BRA 02       ; repeat
08  HLT
09  DAT 0        ; N
10  DAT 1        ; the constant 1
blocks.caption: Program: count down from an input number

blocks.content: A table that records the **values of variables (and registers/memory) after each step** of an algorithm, used to **dry-run** it: to find its output, check that it is correct and locate logic errors.

blocks.title: Trace of the count-down program with input 3

blocks.content:
total ← 0
FOR x ← 0 TO 3
    IF x MOD 2 <> 0 THEN
        total ← total + x * 2
    ELSE
        total ← total + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT x
OUTPUT total
blocks.caption: Trace this algorithm

blocks.title: How to complete a trace table
items: Make a column for **every variable**, condition and output (and the line number if asked).
Write the **initial values** in the first row.
Execute **one statement at a time**; write a value only in the column that changes.
For loops, check the condition each time; for branches, follow the jump.
The **last rows** show the final values and the output.

blocks.content: Common traps: `BRP` jumps when ACC is **zero too**; `MOD` gives the **remainder** (7 MOD 2 = 1); a `FOR` loop's variable takes the **last value** in the range. Write values in a new row each time they change.
